extracted.intended_audience: citizens, delegates, and politically engaged readers considering the ratification and nature of the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Provide principled tests and interpretive rules to decide whether a proposed constitution (or government) is republican, federal, or national in character, and to judge whether a convention was authorized to propose the changes. Focuses on foundation, sources, operation, extent, amendment mode, and the justification of extraordinary measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republican form — definition and essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic is a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior. It is ESSENTIAL that it be derived from the great body of society (not a favored class); it is SUFFICIENT that officers be appointed directly or indirectly by the people and hold their appointments by one of the tenures specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative guidance and examples: the House elected immediately by the people, the Senate appointed indirectly, the President chosen by compound election, judges holding by good behavior; prohibition of titles of nobility and guaranty of republican form to States are decisive marks. Comparisons to state constitutions (e.g., terms of office, impeachment provisions) are used to show conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — foundation (how the constitution is established)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the constitution is founded on the assent/ratification of the people as one aggregate nation or as the several distinct and independent States (i.e., whether assent is the act of each State as a sovereign body).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the act establishing the Constitution results from the assent of the several States (each as a sovereign unit), it is a FEDERAL act; if it results from the majority of the whole people, it would be NATIONAL. The mode of ratification (by State conventions vs by aggregate popular vote) is decisive here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — sources of ordinary powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine from what sources the ordinary powers of each branch are derived: e.g., House of Representatives from the people (national), Senate from the States (federal), Executive from a compound source (both), Judiciary indirectly from the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare each branch to the analogous state practice and note the appointment method: where representation and appointment flow from the people, the feature is national; where they flow from States as political bodies, the feature is federal. The government can be mixed if different branches derive powers from different sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — operation of powers (on states vs individuals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the government's powers operate primarily on political bodies (the States, in their political capacities) or on individual citizens (in their individual capacities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If powers act on individuals (e.g., ordinary legislation affecting persons and property), this points to a NATIONAL character. If powers act on States as collective bodies or on matters exclusively between political entities, this points to a FEDERAL character. Note that many governments will present a mixture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — extent of powers / jurisdictional scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the national authority claims an indefinite supremacy over persons and things (national) or whether its jurisdiction is confined to enumerated objects leaving residuary sovereignty to the States (federal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A truly national government implies general supremacy and control over local authorities; a federal government has enumerated powers with local authorities retaining independent jurisdiction in unenumerated spheres. Disputed boundary cases require impartial tribunals and constitutional rules to prevent conflict or dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — authoritative mode for future changes (amendment/ratification rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the procedure by which future changes or the adoption itself are to be made: whether amendments or adoption depend on the will of the majority of the people (national) or on concurrence of the States (federal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute proportions by STATES versus by CITIZENS. A requirement of concurrence by states (or counting approvals by states rather than aggregate citizens) moves the system toward a FEDERAL character; permitting a less-than-unanimous number of states to bind all moves it toward NATIONAL. Mixed modes (e.g., more than a majority but counted by states) produce a mixed character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive rules for construing the convention's commission
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding the scope of delegated powers given to a convention, apply two construction rules: (1) every part of the expression should, if possible, be given some meaning and contribute to a common end; (2) where parts cannot coincide, the less important should yield to the more important — means sacrificed to ends, not ends to means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these rules to decide whether 'alterations and further provisions' must be read narrowly or broadly. Preference is given to constructions that allow the convention to achieve its essential end (an adequate government to preserve the Union) rather than to literal readings that frustrate that end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing alteration versus transmutation (did the convention exceed its authority?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish changes that amount to authorized 'alterations and further provisions' in the Articles of Confederation from changes that amount to a 'transmutation' (fundamental change) of the government. The question is where the boundary lies between permissible reform and usurpation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted acts include changing titles, inserting new articles, and altering provisions when necessary to achieve the convention's stated end. To determine excess, ask whether 'fundamental principles' of the Confederation have been abandoned (e.g., treating States as non-sovereign, changing appointment sources radically, converting powers that act on States into powers acting directly on individuals). The burden is on critics to mark the precise boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of ratification as a legitimacy test
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the proposed mode of ratification (e.g., confirmation by state legislatures vs confirmation by the people / state conventions and whether a supermajority of states suffices) affects the legitimacy and regularity of the convention's proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the convention departs from strict textual instructions (e.g., reporting a plan to be confirmed by the people and carried into effect by nine states rather than all legislatures), practical considerations (preventing a single obstructionist state from vetoing the will of the many) and historical precedent may mitigate the objection. This factor is important but may be outweighed by the end sought (preserving the Union).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity and duty as justifications for informal or unauthorized propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether urgent public necessity, widespread expectation, and prior precedents can justify actions by delegates or conventions that exceed strict formal authority (i.e., whether duty arising from a crisis can supply defect of regular authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors supporting such justification include a clear and pressing national crisis, universal public expectation of reform, historical instances where informal assumptions of power were accepted (committees, congresses, conventions formed for urgent ends), and the fact that the proposed plan will ultimately stand or fall by the people's approbation. When the end is essential (preservation of the Union), forms may be allowed to give way to substance.
